final_answer:
When an mRNA vaccine is injected, it enters the body and is taken up by cells at the injection site, typically muscle cells. The mRNA is encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles to protect it and facilitate cellular uptake. Once inside the cell, the mRNA is used as a template by the cell’s ribosomes to produce viral proteins, such as the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2. These proteins are then displayed on the cell surface or secreted. The immune system recognizes these proteins as foreign, triggering an immune response. Dendritic cells and other antigen-presenting cells capture the spike protein and present it to T cells and B cells. B cells produce antibodies specific to the spike protein, while T cells help coordinate the immune response and destroy infected cells. The mRNA is degraded by the cell after its instructions are completed, ensuring it does not integrate into the genome. This process primes the immune system to recognize and combat the actual virus if encountered later, leading to long-term immunity.
